danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 6
paragraphs: Blandt de utallige kategorier, man kan anvende på fænomenerne i menneskelivet, kan man skelne mellem dem, hvor substansen er det afgørende, og dem, hvor formen er det afgørende. Til den sidstnævnte — til forskel fra landsbylivet, landlivet, provinslivet eller selv moskvaer-livet — kan vi henregne petersborglivet og især livet i dets saloner. Det salonliv er uforanderligt. Siden 1805 havde vi sluttet fred og atter strides med Bonaparte, vi havde lavet forfatninger og ophævet dem igen, men Anna Pavlovnas og Hélènes saloner forblev nøjagtigt som de havde været — den ene syv, den anden fem år tidligere. Hos Anna Pavlovna talte man med forvirring om Bonapartes triumfer, nøjagtigt som før, og så i dem og i den underdanighed, de europæiske monarker viste ham, en ondsindet sammensværgelse, hvis eneste formål var at skabe ubehag og ængstelighed for den hofkreds, som Anna Pavlovna repræsenterede. Og i Hélènes salon, som Rumjantsev selv beærede med sine besøg og betragtede Hélène som en bemærkelsesværdigt intelligent kvinde, talte man med den samme begejstring i 1812 som i 1808 om den »store nation« og den »store mand« og beklagede vort brud med Frankrig, et brud, der ifølge dem snarest burde afsluttes med fred.

I den seneste tid, siden kejserens tilbagekomst fra hæren, havde der været nogen ophidselse i disse stridende salonkredse og visse fjendtlige demonstrationer mod hinanden, men hvert lejr bevarede sin egen tendens. I Anna Pavlovnas kreds optog man kun de franskmænd, der var dybt rodfæstede legitimister, og der blev givet udtryk for patriotiske synspunkter, nemlig at man ikke burde gå i det franske teater, og at opretholdelsen af den franske teatertrup kostede staten lige så meget som et helt armékorps. Krigens forløb blev fulgt ivrigt, og kun de mest smigrende rapporter om vores hær blev sat i omløb. I den franske kreds omkring Hélène og Rumjantsev blev beretningerne om fjendens grusomhed og krigen modsagt, og alle Napoleons fredsforsøg blev diskuteret. I den kreds så man ned på dem, der rådede til hastigt at forberede overflytningen til Kazan af hoffet og pigeuddannelsesinstitutterne under enkekejserindens beskyttelse. I Hélènes kreds blev krigen i det hele taget betragtet som en række formelle demonstrationer, der snart ville ende med fred, og man delte den opfattelse, som Bilibin udtrykte — Bilibin, der nu var helt hjemme i Hélènes hus i Petersborg, som ethvert klogt menneske var forpligtet til at besøge — at sagen ikke ville blive afgjort med krudt, men af dem der opfandt det. I den kreds blev Moskvas begejstring — nyheden herom var nået til Petersborg samtidig med kejserens tilbagekomst — latterliggjort sarkastisk og meget klogt, men med stor forsigtighed.

Anna Pavlovnas kreds derimod var henrykt over denne begejstring og talte om den, som Plutark taler om de gamles bedrifter. Fyrst Vasilij, der stadig beklædte sine forhenværende vigtige poster, udgjorde et bindeled mellem disse to kredse. Han besøgte sin »gode veninde Anna Pavlovna« såvel som sin datters »diplomatiske salon«, og i sin stadige pendlen mellem de to lejre blev han ofte forvirret og sagde hos Hélène, hvad han burde have sagt hos Anna Pavlovna, og omvendt.

Kort efter kejserens tilbagekomst fordømte fyrst Vasilij i en samtale om krigen hos Anna Pavlovna skarpt Barclay de Tolly, men var i tvivl om, hvem der burde udnævnes til øverstkommanderende. En af gæsterne, sædvanligvis omtalt som »en mand af store fortjenester«, der havde fortalt, hvordan han den dag havde set Kutuzov (den nyvalgte chef for Petersborgs milits) præsidere over indskrivningen af rekrutter i Finansministeriet, vovede forsigtigt at antyde, at Kutuzov ville være manden, der tilfredsstillede alle krav.
Anna Pavlovna bemærkede med et melankolsk smil, at Kutuzov ikke havde gjort andet end at forvolde kejseren ærgrelse.
»Jeg har talt og talt ved Adelsforsamlingen,« afbrød fyrst Vasilij, »men de lyttede ikke til mig. Jeg sagde dem, at hans valg til militsens chef ikke ville behage kejseren. De lyttede ikke til mig.«

»Det er al den mani for opposition,« fortsatte han. »Og for hvem? Det hele skyldes, at vi vil efterabe moskovitternes tåbelige begejstring,« fortsatte fyrst Vasilij og glemte et øjeblik, at skønt man hos Hélène skulle latterliggøre Moskvas begejstring, skulle man hos Anna Pavlovna være ekstatisk over den. Men han rettede sin fejl på stedet. »Nå, er det passende, at grev Kutuzov, Ruslands ældste general, skulle præsidere over den domstol? Han får intet ud af sin møje! Hvordan kan de gøre en mand til øverstkommanderende, der ikke kan sidde til hest, falder i søvn ved et krigsråd og har de allerværste sæder! Et godt ry, han skabte sig i Bukarest! Jeg taler ikke om hans evner som general, men i en tid som denne — at udnævne en affældig, blind gammel mand, direkte blind? En god idé at have en blind general! Han kan ikke se noget. At spille blindebuk? Han kan overhovedet ikke se!«
Ingen svarede på hans bemærkninger.

Det var helt korrekt den fire og tyvende juli. Men den ni og tyvende juli modtog Kutuzov titlen fyrste. Det kunne antyde et ønske om at slippe af med ham, og derfor var fyrst Vasilijs mening stadig korrekt, skønt han nu ikke havde hastværk med at udtrykke den. Men den ottende august mødtes et udvalg bestående af feltmarskal Saltykov, Araktjejev, Vjazmitinov, Lopukhin og Kotjubej for at drøfte krigens forløb. Udvalget nåede til den slutning, at vore nederlag skyldtes mangel på enhed i kommandoen, og skønt udvalgets medlemmer var klar over kejserens modvilje mod Kutuzov, enedes de efter kort drøftelse om at anbefale hans udnævnelse til øverstkommanderende. Samme dag blev Kutuzov udnævnt til øverstkommanderende med fuld magt over hærene og hele det besatte område.

Den niende august mødte fyrst Vasilij hos Anna Pavlovna atter »manden af store fortjenester.« Denne var meget opmærksom over for Anna Pavlovna, fordi han ønskede at blive udnævnt til direktør for en af pigeuddannelsesanstalterne. Fyrst Vasilij kom ind i salen med minen af en lykkelig sejrherre, der har opnået sit mål.

»Nå, har I hørt den store nyhed? Fyrst Kutuzov er feltmarskal! Al splid er forbi! Jeg er så glad, så henrykt! Endelig har vi en mand!« sagde han og sendte et strengt og betydningsfuldt blik rundt i stuen.

»Manden af store fortjenester« kunne, trods sit ønske om at opnå posten som direktør, ikke afholde sig fra at minde fyrst Vasilij om hans tidligere holdning. Skønt dette var uhøfligt over for fyrst Vasilij i Anna Pavlovnas salon og også over for Anna Pavlovna selv, der havde modtaget nyheden med glæde, kunne han ikke modstå fristelsen.
»Men, fyrste, de siger han er blind!« sagde han og mindede fyrst Vasilij om hans egne ord.
»Pyt! Vrøvl! Han ser udmærket,« sagde fyrst Vasilij hurtigt, med dyb stemme og et let host — den stemme og det host, hvormed han plejede at afvise alle vanskeligheder.

»Han ser udmærket,« tilføjede han. »Og det, jeg er så glad for,« fortsatte han, »er, at vores suveræn har givet ham fuld magt over alle hærene og hele området — beføjelser, ingen øverstkommanderende nogen sinde har haft før. Han er en anden enevældsmonark,« sluttede han med et sejrssmil.
»Gud give det! Gud give det!« sagde Anna Pavlovna.
»Manden af store fortjenester«, der stadig var en novice i hofkredse og ønskede at smigre Anna Pavlovna ved at forsvare hendes tidligere holdning til dette spørgsmål, bemærkede:

»Der siges, at kejseren var modvillig til at give Kutuzov disse beføjelser. De siger, han rødmede som en pige, der får Joconde læst op, da han sagde til Kutuzov: 'Deres kejser og fædrelandet tildeler Dem denne ære.'«
»Måske havde hjertet ingen del i den tale,« sagde Anna Pavlovna.

»Å nej, nej!« svarede fyrst Vasilij varmt — han ville nu ikke give Kutuzov fra sig til nogen; efter hans mening var Kutuzov ikke blot beundringsværdig selv, men tilbedt af alle. »Nej, det er umuligt,« sagde han, »for vores suveræn satte så stor pris på ham tidligere.«
»Gid blot fyrst Kutuzov påtager sig den virkelige magt og ikke lader nogen stikke en kæp i hjulet,« bemærkede Anna Pavlovna.
Fyrst Vasilij, der straks forstod, hvem hun hentydede til, sagde hviskende:
»Jeg véd med sikkerhed, at Kutuzov stillede det som en ufravigelig betingelse, at tronfølgeren ikke skulle være hos hæren. Ved I, hvad han sagde til kejseren?«
Og fyrst Vasilij gentog de ord, Kutuzov angiveligt skulle have sagt til kejseren. »Jeg kan hverken straffe ham, hvis han handler forkert, eller belønne ham, hvis han handler rigtigt.«
»Å, en meget klog mand er fyrst Kutuzov! Jeg har kendt ham længe!«

»De siger endda,« bemærkede »manden af store fortjenester«, der endnu ikke besad den rette hovtakt, »at hans excellence stillede det som en udtrykkelig betingelse, at suverænen selv ikke skulle være hos hæren.«
Så snart han sagde dette, vendte både fyrst Vasilij og Anna Pavlovna sig fra ham og kiggede bedrøvet på hinanden med et suk over hans naivitet.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 6
paragraphs: Among the countless categories that can be applied to the phenomena of human life, one may distinguish between those where substance matters most and those where form does. To the latter—as distinct from village, country, provincial, or even Moscow life—we may assign Petersburg life, and especially the life of its salons. That salon life is unchanging. Since 1805 we had made peace and quarreled again with Bonaparte and had made constitutions and unmade them, but the salons of Anna Pavlovna and Helene remained exactly as they had been—one seven and the other five years before. At Anna Pavlovna's they spoke with puzzlement of Bonaparte's successes, just as before, and saw in them and in the European sovereigns' submission to him a malicious conspiracy whose sole purpose was to cause unpleasantness and anxiety to the court circle that Anna Pavlovna represented. And in Helene's salon, which Rumyantsev himself honored with his visits, regarding Helene as a remarkably intelligent woman, they spoke with the same enthusiasm in 1812 as in 1808 of the "great nation" and the "great man" and regretted our rift with France, a rift which, according to them, ought to be promptly ended by peace.

Lately, since the Emperor's return from the army, there had been some excitement in these rival salon circles and some demonstrations of hostility between them, but each camp kept to its own line. In Anna Pavlovna's circle, only those Frenchmen who were dyed-in-the-wool royalists were admitted, and patriotic views were expressed: that one shouldn't attend the French theater and that maintaining the French troupe was costing the government as much as a whole army corps. The war's progress was eagerly followed, and only the most flattering reports about our army were circulated. In the French circle of Helene and Rumyantsev, reports of the enemy's cruelty and of the war were challenged, and all Napoleon's attempts at conciliation were discussed. In that circle they frowned on those who advised hurried preparations for moving the court and the girls' educational institutions under the Dowager Empress's patronage to Kazan. In Helene's circle, the war was regarded as a series of formal demonstrations that would very soon end in peace, and the view expressed by Bilibin—who was now quite at home in Helene's house, which every clever man was expected to visit—prevailed: that matters would be settled not by gunpowder but by those who invented it. In that circle, the Moscow enthusiasm (news of which had reached Petersburg along with the Emperor's return) was ridiculed sarcastically and very cleverly, though with great caution.

Anna Pavlovna's circle, on the contrary, was enraptured by this enthusiasm and spoke of it as Plutarch speaks of the deeds of the ancients. Prince Vasili, who still held his former important posts, formed a connecting link between the two circles. He visited his "good friend Anna Pavlovna" as well as his daughter's "diplomatic salon," and in his constant shuttling between the two camps often got confused, saying at Helene's what he should have said at Anna Pavlovna's, and vice versa.

Soon after the Emperor's return, Prince Vasili, in a conversation about the war at Anna Pavlovna's, severely criticized Barclay de Tolly but was undecided as to who ought to be appointed commander in chief. One of the visitors, usually referred to as "a man of great merit," having described how he had that day seen Kutuzov—the newly chosen chief of the Petersburg militia—presiding over the enrollment of recruits at the Treasury, cautiously suggested that Kutuzov might be the man to satisfy all requirements.
Anna Pavlovna remarked with a melancholy smile that Kutuzov had done nothing but cause the Emperor annoyance.

"I've talked and talked at the Assembly of the Nobility," Prince Vasili interrupted, "but they wouldn't listen to me. I told them his election as chief of the militia would not please the Emperor. They didn't listen."

"It's all this mania for opposition," he went on. "And for whom? It's all because we want to imitate the foolish enthusiasm of those Muscovites," Prince Vasili continued, forgetting for a moment that at Helene's one had to ridicule Moscow's enthusiasm, while at Anna Pavlovna's one had to be rapturous about it. But he corrected himself at once. "Now, is it fitting that Count Kutuzov, the oldest general in Russia, should preside at that tribunal? He'll get nothing for his trouble! How could they make a man commander in chief who can't mount a horse, who falls asleep in council, and has the very worst morals? A fine reputation he made at Bucharest! I don't speak of his capacity as a general, but at a time like this how can they appoint a decrepit, blind old man—positively blind? A fine idea, a blind general! He can't see a thing. Playing blindman's buff? He can't see at all!"
No one responded to his remarks.

This was perfectly correct on the twenty-fourth of July. But on the twenty-ninth of July, Kutuzov was given the title of Prince. This might indicate a wish to get rid of him, and so Prince Vasili's opinion remained valid, though he was in no hurry to repeat it. But on the eighth of August, a committee consisting of Field Marshal Saltykov, Arakcheev, Vyazmitinov, Lopukhin, and Kochubey met to consider the progress of the war. This committee concluded that our failures were due to a lack of unified command, and though its members were aware of the Emperor's dislike of Kutuzov, after brief deliberation they agreed to recommend his appointment as commander in chief. That same day Kutuzov was appointed commander in chief with full powers over the armies and over the entire region they occupied.

On the ninth of August, Prince Vasili met the "man of great merit" again at Anna Pavlovna's. The latter was very attentive to Anna Pavlovna because he wanted to be appointed director of one of the girls' educational institutions. Prince Vasili entered the room with the air of a happy conqueror who has achieved the object of his desires.

"Well, have you heard the great news? Prince Kutuzov is field marshal! All disagreements are over! I am so glad, so delighted! At last we have a real leader!" he said, glancing sternly and significantly around the drawing room.

The "man of great merit," despite his desire for the director's post, couldn't resist reminding Prince Vasili of his former opinion. Though this was impolite to Prince Vasili in Anna Pavlovna's drawing room, and also to Anna Pavlovna herself, who had received the news with delight, he couldn't resist the temptation.
"But, Prince, they say he's blind!" he said, echoing Prince Vasili's own words.
"Nonsense! He sees well enough," said Prince Vasili quickly, in a deep voice with a slight cough—the voice and cough he always used to dismiss difficulties.

"He sees well enough," he repeated. "And what I'm so pleased about is that our sovereign has given him full powers over all the armies and the whole region—powers no commander in chief has ever had before. He's a second autocrat," he concluded with a triumphant smile.
"God grant it! God grant it!" said Anna Pavlovna.
The "man of great merit," who was still a newcomer to court circles, wishing to flatter Anna Pavlovna by defending her earlier position on this question, observed:

"They say the Emperor was reluctant to give Kutuzov those powers. They say he blushed like a girl being read a romantic novel when he said to Kutuzov: 'Your Emperor and the Fatherland award you this honor.'"
"Perhaps the heart had no part in that speech," said Anna Pavlovna.

"Oh, no, no!" Prince Vasili warmly objected, now unwilling to yield Kutuzov to anyone; in his opinion Kutuzov was not only admirable but was adored by everybody. "No, that's impossible," he said, "for our sovereign valued him so highly before."
"God grant only that Prince Kutuzov assumes real power and doesn't let anyone put a spoke in his wheel," observed Anna Pavlovna.
Immediately understanding who she meant, Prince Vasili said in a whisper:
"I know for a fact that Kutuzov made it an absolute condition that the Tsarevich should not be with the army. Do you know what he said to the Emperor?"
And Prince Vasili repeated the words supposedly spoken by Kutuzov to the Emperor: "I can neither punish him if he does wrong nor reward him if he does right."
"Oh, a very wise man is Prince Kutuzov! I have known him a long time!"
"They even say," remarked the "man of great merit," who had not yet mastered courtly tact, "that his excellency made it an express condition that the sovereign himself should not be with the army."
As soon as he said this, both Prince Vasili and Anna Pavlovna turned away from him and glanced sadly at one another with a sigh at his naivety.
